# Count enough to certify the answer, not necessarily to generate the group

27 September 2026. Continuation of notes 22 and 23 on
`research/prx-quantum-phase2`, from commit
`4a22c36b249a69bd172fe5c47b988e02c91c52c8`. Manuscript remains on hold.

**Result:** the bounded completion can be applied to the subgroup generated by
whatever elements were actually obtained. Its exact size supplies a stronger
cardinality divisor than their order lcm alone. When the rigorous ambient interval
contains just one multiple of that size, the ambient answer is exact even if the
sampled elements do not generate the ambient group.

This is a combination and application of existing group-order ingredients, not
a new quantum primitive, a new general subgroup algorithm, or an advantage claim.
The [executable diagnostic](../../experiments/subgroup_stop_v1/README.md) tests
this distinction without assuming complete sampling or enumerating a large group.

## 1. The acceptance lemma

Let G be a finite abelian group, with correct explicit group operations and a
rigorous interval L <= N = |G| <= U. Let D_1,...,D_k be any elements of G. Write

$$
H=\langle D_1,\ldots,D_k\rangle,\qquad M=|H|.
$$

No assertion that H=G is made. Suppose M has been computed exactly. Define

$$
a=\left\lceil\frac{L}{M}\right\rceil,\qquad
b=\left\lfloor\frac{U}{M}\right\rfloor.
$$

If a=b, return N=aM. If a<b, return inconclusive. If a>b, the bounds and the
claimed subgroup size are inconsistent. In particular, **do not return M merely
because the subgroup computation has finished**.

Proof: Lagrange's theorem gives M|N, so the positive integer N/M belongs to
[a,b]. A singleton interval fixes it. This implication does not involve a
sampling distribution or a generation-confidence bound. It is a sufficient
arithmetic acceptance test, not a claim that no stronger test is available.

The bounds themselves remain premises. An incorrect interval can produce an
incorrect answer despite completely correct subgroup arithmetic. Membership of
the input elements in the intended group and correct canonical group operations
must also be justified by the group implementation.

## 2. Why note 23 works for an incomplete ambient list

Certify the exact order r_i of every supplied D_i, using a complete proved-prime
factorization, r_i D_i=0, and (r_i/ell)D_i != 0 for every prime ell dividing r_i.
Then

$$
E=\operatorname{lcm}(r_1,\ldots,r_k)=\exp(H),\qquad
C=\left\lfloor\frac{U}{E}\right\rfloor.
$$

The supplied list is a complete generating list of H by definition. We know
M<=U, hence M/E<=C. This is all that note 23's bounded completion needs; an
ambient lower bound is not a required bound on H. It would be invalid to use L
as a lower bound on M when the list might be incomplete.

For every prime ell>C in E, an additional ell factor in M/E is impossible.
Consequently the ell-primary part of H is cyclic of the known order ell^e.
This statement concerns H, not the corresponding component of G. Primes of G
may be wholly absent from E.

Let E_s be the product of prime powers of E whose primes are <=C, and set
E_b=E/E_s. The projected generators E_b D_i generate H_s. For each small prime,
choose a D_i whose order attains ell^e, and set A_ell=(E/ell^e)D_i. The sum A of
these A_ell has order E_s. Thus H_s/<A> has exactly M/E cosets.

Membership in <A> is tested with the ordinary prime-power digit method. In a
prime-power component with anchor a of order ell^e, compare the successively
scaled residuals with the ell multiples of ell^(e-1)a; subtract the found
digits times ell^j a, and require a zero final residual. A missing digit or a
nonzero residual rejects membership. No prior membership promise is used.
The different prime-power projections jointly separate the whole E_s-torsion
part, so membership holds exactly when it holds in every component.

Start with the identity coset, repeatedly add each projected generator, and
retain a representative only when the membership test distinguishes its coset
from every existing one. Every representative lies in H_s by its construction.
At termination the representatives are pairwise inequivalent and closed under
the generating list. In a finite group, closure under these positive additions
also covers inverses. Thus they are exactly H_s/<A>, not a partial orbit.
Multiplying their count by E returns M, not N.

The branch first tries note 22's cheaper E-divisor test. If it already succeeds,
no subgroup completion is needed. A predeclared C cap bounds the optional
completion; exceeding it requests more information or the established fallback.
It is not evidence of mathematical infeasibility.

## 3. Less sampling is permitted, not automatically cheaper

Let Delta=U-L. The condition M>Delta is sufficient for acceptance: an interval
of width Delta cannot contain two distinct multiples of M. Equality is not
sufficient; [2,4] contains two multiples of 2. The exact a=b test can also
succeed when this sufficient width condition does not hold.

Writing d=[G:H], it suffices that d<N/Delta when Delta>0. In the large-field
Weil interval, the leading ratio Delta/N is about 4g/sqrt(Q), so full generation
can be a stronger requirement than this arithmetic stopping condition. This
is a conditional scale comparison, not a probability statement about sampled
curve points or a prescribed distribution of d.

There is a compensating cost. Put c_H=M/E. The computable completion parameter is

$$
C=\left\lfloor\frac{U}{N}\,d\,c_H\right\rfloor.
$$

In the U<2N regime proved in note 23 (in particular its sufficient Q>=64g^2
setup),

$$
dc_H\le C<2dc_H.
$$

Thus C is within a factor two of **d times the subgroup's cyclic index**, not
of c_H alone. A smaller sampled subgroup can make the declared completion
budget larger. Removing an ambient-generation requirement does not make the
missing structure free or establish a reduction in total gate count.

After exact order/factorization verification, the conservative group-operation
bound of note 23 applies unchanged with this C: for B=max(1,ceil(log2 E)),
O(k C^2 (B^2+C B)+k B^2+C B) group/equality operations and
O(CB+C+k) stored group elements, plus integer arithmetic. This is polynomial
in the value of C, not in log C. The implementation does linear equality lookup;
no coherent hash table or QRAM access is assumed. Factoring, primality checking,
order acquisition, group encoding, and any failed acquisition/completion rounds
are additional real costs. The diagnostic's trial-division primality test is
exact but is not the polynomial-bit-time proof verifier contemplated by the
abstract factored-order model.

## 4. Two explicit distinctions

For G=(Z/2)^3 and two independent supplied elements, E=2 and M=4. In [6,10],
the E-divisor candidates are 6,8,10, but the sole M-multiple is 8. The answer is
certified although H has index two. In [4,12], the same M leaves 4,8,12 and
must remain inconclusive. This repairs the interpretation of note 23's
incomplete-list control without claiming that its stated complete-list theorem
was incorrect.

A large-integer execution control uses
G=Z/(101*2^e) x Z/4 x Z/2 x Z/3, with e=20,40,80, and supplies only the first
three coordinate generators. Their subgroup has M=8E, with E=101*2^e, whereas
N=24E. The separately supplied interval [N-2E,N+2E] gives C=26. Completion counts
eight cosets using a two-entry digit table and skips prime 101; the unique
M-multiple in the interval is 3M=N. Prime 3 was not in the sampled order support.
No list of the enormous ambient group is constructed.

The control's interval is deliberately built using its known answer, and its
coordinate presentation already makes that answer trivial classically. This is
an algebraic regression control, NOT an independently justified workload,
performance comparison, evidence of quantum utility, or practical input source.

## 5. What changes in the quantum workflow

The accepted branch is now:

    obtain elements and candidate orders within a declared acquisition budget
    -> verify exact orders and required factorizations
    -> try the lcm-divisor interval test
    -> if affordable, count the generated subgroup with bounded completion
    -> accept only a unique multiple in the original rigorous ambient interval
    -> otherwise acquire more information or use the established fallback.

For this early-acceptance branch, incomplete or nonuniform sampling cannot by
itself cause a false cardinality. Sampling affects whether and when the test
accepts. There is no generation-confidence term needed to justify an accepted
integer once its group/order/interval premises have been checked. Quantum order
proposals that fail exact verification are rejected or retried, not silently
promoted to divisors. This is not a guarantee of termination, a lower sample
count, or a claim that the fallback has become deterministic.

Apply the same rule separately to each required extension-field/twist
cardinality. When every required count is accepted, the preceding exact zeta
reconstruction can use them. This does not change the reconstruction's own
premises or resolve its priority. All general Jacobian controlled translations,
field extensions, measurement, factorization and fallback costs remain.

The classical competitor receives precisely the same stopping rule and subgroup
methods, as well as specialized point-counting methods that bypass this route.
Any eventual advantage must survive that comparison in the remaining period
acquisition and complete workflow, not come from denying these deductions.

## 6. Verification and provenance

The new independent diagnostic checks 662 supplied lists on eleven small direct
products. It includes every ordered list of lengths zero, one and two, plus the
rank-three basis. Of these lists, 404 generate a proper ambient subgroup.
It compares 1,986 completions to independent full subgroup enumeration and
3,310 ambient-interval decisions to explicit integer-multiple enumeration.
All accepted decisions equal the independently known ambient size. It rejects
1,236 deliberately nonminimal orders, plus eight malformed order/factor cases.
Three large controls, the wide-interval negative control, a strict-width boundary,
an inconsistent-divisor control and the C-cap fallback are retained.

The five interval policies include singleton intervals and repeated bounds on
tiny cases. Their accepted counts are bookkeeping, not a discovery success rate.
Every order is supplied classically in these diagnostics. There is no actual
quantum order acquisition, curve sampler, field-extension run, large-curve
point counter or hardware experiment. The generic routine receives only group
operations and supplied order/bound data; the reference fixture knows the
coordinates/cardinality solely to construct controls and independently check them.

The predecessor archive was located in the Library, but its raw-byte
materialization failed. No inherited helper was reconstructed and mislabeled as
an import. The new code is independently written from the stated mathematics.
The 164-curve archive suite and the repository's historical root verifier were
not rerun. New source/report hashes and the repeatable standalone verifier are
committed with this note, so this continuation does not depend on a new
uncommitted source archive.

## 7. Contribution boundary and next decision

Sutherland's exponent-first algorithms, prime-primary structure methods, and
tight-bound cardinality reasoning are strong prior classical ingredients [1,2].
Lagrange's theorem and the unique-multiple argument are elementary. This note
claims an exact correction to the current workflow's required premise and
acceptance semantics, not originality for those ingredients. It has not
established a standalone publishable result.

The next question is no longer how to wrap another exact stopping test. It is
whether a justified curve/invariant family leaves a consequential period-finding
cost after these classical reductions, and whether complete reversible general
Jacobian arithmetic makes the quantum route competitive. A family-level
comparison or an actual controlled-translation resource bound is the next
scientific gate. Further small abstract groups do not answer it. The broader
compact-input direction stays open; manuscript preparation remains on hold.
